lesson.title: The idea: why PCA chases variance
lesson.lead: Explained as if you are 10, then on the slides' maths. `Lecture_12.pdf` p. 2–8.

blocks.text: **Picture it.** You have a cloud of dots on paper. You may keep only **one number** per dot instead of two. So you draw a line, drop each dot straight onto it (its **shadow**), and keep only where the shadow lands. Which line loses the least? The one where the shadows are **most spread out**, because spread-out shadows still tell the dots apart. Shadows bunched together lose almost everything.

**Spread = variance.** So PCA's question is: which direction makes the shadows' variance as large as possible? That direction is the **first principal component (PC1)**. The second (PC2) is the best direction at right angles to PC1, and so on.

items: Turn the line: the spread V(θ) on the right goes up and down.
Its highest point is **λ₁** and happens exactly along the top eigenvector of S. Its lowest point is **λ₂**, exactly 90° away.
So "the line with the biggest spread" and "the eigenvector of the biggest eigenvalue" are the same thing. Lecture 12 proves this with a Lagrangian.

lesson.title: Type 2 · Why PC1 is an eigenvector: the Lagrangian proof
lesson.lead: `Lecture_12.pdf` p. 9–23. Same Lagrange method as Lecture 11.

groups.label: Constrained problem
groups.note: Without the constraint, a longer b₁ gives a bigger number forever: only the direction should count.

groups.label: Lagrangian
groups.note: So b₁ must be an eigenvector of S, and λ (the multiplier) is its eigenvalue.

groups.label: Which eigenvector
groups.note: The variance along an eigenvector equals its eigenvalue, so take the **largest** λ.

groups.label: M components
lines: [b₁ … b_M]: eigenvectors of the M largest λ
groups.note: Each next PC is the best direction perpendicular to the ones already chosen; S is symmetric, so its eigenvectors are perpendicular (spectral theorem).

blocks.text: **Why ∇f = λ∇g (p. 14–15):** at the best point on the circle ‖b‖ = 1, moving along the circle cannot improve f, so ∇f has no part along the circle. ∇g is also perpendicular to the circle. Two vectors perpendicular to the same direction (in 2-D) are parallel: ∇f = λ∇g.

blocks.label: Where marks are lost
blocks.text: Differentiating the constraint as λb instead of 2λb · forgetting ‖b‖ = 1 · saying Var = λ for a vector that is not unit length (then Var = λ‖b‖²).

items: **Do:** P41, then Companion Q2 (mark the student's work).

worked.title: Full PCA · Mar 2026 Q5: covariance, eigenvectors, principal subspace (7 marks)

problem.text: Rows are observations: X = [[0, 3], [1, 5], [2, 7]]. (1) Compute the covariance matrix S. [2M] (2) Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of S. [3M] (3) Find the 1-dimensional principal subspace. [2M]

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: The full PCA recipe on three 2-D points: centre → S → eigen → pick the largest. Marks 2 + 3 + 2.

steps.label: Plan of attack
steps.text:
1. Mean of each column, subtract it.
2. S = (1/N)X_cᵀX_c.
3. det(S − λI) = 0, then (S − λI)v = 0 for each λ.
4. The eigenvector of the largest λ spans the principal subspace.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: This paper's symbols are kept. **S** (or **Σ**, **C**) = covariance matrix, **λ** = an eigenvalue of S (**not** a Lagrange multiplier here), **v**, **q**, **α**, **b**, **e** = a unit eigenvector = a principal direction, **z** = a point's score (its coordinate along the direction).

steps.label: STEP 6 · Principal subspace  [2M]
steps.text:
Largest eigenvalue 10/3 ⇒ **span{(1, 2)}**, the line through the mean in direction (1, 2).
λ₂ = 0: all three points lie exactly on that line, so PC1 keeps 100% of the variance.
Scores (centred) along (1, 2)/√5: −√5, 0, √5.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:
• Not centring before building S.
• Picking the eigenvector of λ = 0.
• Not saying which divisor (1/N or 1/(N − 1)) you used.

worked.title: Derive · Sourabh P41: first principal component through a Lagrangian

problem.text: A 2-D random vector has covariance Σ = [[5, 2], [2, 2]]. The first PC is Y₁ = αᵀX with αᵀα = 1. (a) Write the constrained problem and its Lagrangian. (b) Show the stationarity condition is Σα = λα and that Var(Y₁) = λ there. (c) Find α for PC1 and PC2 and their variances. (d) The correlation between Y₁ and Y₂ and the share of variance of Y₁. (Saurabh sir's `MFML_ZC416_Solved_Practice_Set.pdf`)

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: PCA as a constrained maximum (Lagrange, Lecture 11) and solving it on numbers.

steps.label: Plan of attack
steps.text: max αᵀΣα s.t. αᵀα = 1 → L → ∇L = 0 → eigen-equation → multiply by αᵀ to get the variance → pick the largest λ.

steps.label: Notation
steps.text: Saurabh sir's symbols: **α** = unit direction (b₁ on the slides), **λ** = the Lagrange multiplier, which turns out to be the eigenvalue, Y = αᵀX = score.

steps.label: STEP 1 · (a) Problem and L
steps.text:
max αᵀΣα s.t. αᵀα = 1
L = αᵀΣα − λ(αᵀα − 1)

steps.label: STEP 2 · (b) Stationarity
steps.text:
∇(αᵀΣα) = 2Σα (Σ symmetric), ∇(αᵀα) = 2α
∇L = 2Σα − 2λα = 0 ⇒ **Σα = λα**: α must be an eigenvector.

steps.label: STEP 3 · (b) Variance = λ
steps.text: Var(Y₁) = αᵀΣα = αᵀ(λα) = λαᵀα = λ ⇒ to maximise, take the **largest** λ.

steps.label: Answers at a glance
steps.text: L = αᵀΣα − λ(αᵀα − 1); Σα = λα, Var = λ; α₁ = (2, 1)/√5 (6), α₂ = (1, −2)/√5 (1); correlation 0; 85.71%.

steps.label: Where marks are lost
steps.text:
• Dropping the 2 on one term only (then the eigen-equation comes out wrong).
• Choosing the smallest eigenvalue.

worked.title: Derive · Companion Q2: find the three faults in a student's derivation (6 marks)

problem.text: Σ = [[5, 2], [2, 8]]. A student writes: (1) max αᵀΣα s.t. αᵀα = 1. (2) L = αᵀΣα − λ(αᵀα − 1). (3) ∂L/∂α = 2Σα − λα = 0, so Σα = ½λα. (4) det(Σ − λI) = λ² − 13λ + 36 ⇒ λ = 9, 4. (5) For λ = 9, α = (1, 2), so Y₁ = X₁ + 2X₂. (6) Var(Y₁) = 9. (a) Find the three faulty lines. [3M] (b) Correct them. [2M] (c) Compute Var(X₁ + 2X₂) directly. [1M] (Companion §15, Question 2)

steps.label: What is tested
steps.text: Knowing the derivation well enough to mark it.

steps.label: STEP 1 · (a) Faults
steps.text:
**(3)** ∂(λαᵀα)/∂α = 2λα, not λα.
**(5)** (1, 2) is not unit length (‖(1, 2)‖ = √5).
**(6)** With the α of line (5), the variance is 45, not 9.
Lines (1), (2), (4) are correct.

steps.label: STEP 3 · (c)
steps.text:
Var(X₁ + 2X₂) = 5 + 4(8) + 4(2) = **45** = (1, 2)Σ(1, 2)ᵀ
In general Var(αᵀX) = λ‖α‖², so Var = λ only for a unit α (here ‖α‖² = 5, 5 × 9 = 45).

steps.label: Answers at a glance
steps.text: Faults in (3), (5), (6); Y₁ = (X₁ + 2X₂)/√5 with variance 9; Var(X₁ + 2X₂) = 45.
